new_statements.quote: 2.10. Word stress. Stress is on the final vowel of the word; if a suffix containing a vowel is added to a word, the stress shifts to this vowel. The evidential particle -tï (see 7.3.2.) is usually unstressed, but the pronunciation changes to -tʊ when it bears emphatic stress. The same applies to the question particle mi (see 7.3.8.) which is realized mʊ when stressed. [p. 35] || 7.3.2: The evidential particle -tï is attached to the predicate noun. When stressed, the particle -tï is realized as -tʊ; in folk tales, the obsolescent form -trʊ may still occur. [p. 149] || 7.3.8: The question particle mi renders an affirmative sentence into an interrogative one, expressing a yes-no question. When stressed, it is pronounced mʊ; older speakers may use the assimilated form pi following plosives. [p. 152]

new_statements.relation_note: Placement is identical to the catalog's 'final' rule (final stress), so it agrees; it refines by stating that stress shifts onto vowel-bearing suffixes (final stress of the suffixed word) and by putting the evidential and question particles outside the stress domain except under emphasis. This is the Glottolog reference grammar and the likely ultimate source of an earlier compilation rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the last vowel (final syllable) of the word, and it moves rightward onto any vowel-bearing suffix that is added, so the stressed syllable is always the final one of the suffixed word. The enclitic evidential particle -tï and the yes-no question particle mi lie outside the stress domain (normally unstressed) and take stress only under emphasis, when their vowel changes to ʊ (-tʊ, mʊ).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned anywhere in the book (full-text scanned search of all 431 pages found no other stress or accent statements).
new_statements.exceptions: The evidential particle -tï and the question particle mi are usually unstressed (they follow the stressed final syllable of the host); under emphatic stress they surface as -tʊ and mʊ. Section 2.11 adds that Chinese tones are not retained in Chinese loanwords. No lexical exceptions to final stress are listed.
new_statements.identity_note: Roos 2000 describes Western Yugur (Turkic, Gansu), the language of this glottocode, based mainly on speakers from Minghua/Dahé districts of Sunan County and on the consultant Zhong Jinwen; it explicitly distinguishes it from Mongolic Eastern Yugur. No dialect-specific stress statement is made.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed final stress, dominant/rightmost: stress moves to the last suffix vowel) rests on the standard reference grammar of the language, Roos 2000 (Leiden PhD, 431 pp.), sec. 2.10 p.35. We previously held no copy; the cited the Internet Archive scan was downloaded now and the quotation confirmed verbatim on the page scan and by scanned. No better stress source exists in the accessible literature: Glottolog's larger items are a Chinese-language grammar (Chen 2004, print only) and Zhong's 2019 ANU thesis (request-only), and the one experimental paper found (Lyu 2019, downloaded) agrees with final, suffix-shifting stress. Nothing suggests a reclassify. The record's grade field is empty and 'held' was empty; with the primary source now obtained by the project and verified, the strength of the evidence can be set to primary-source-verified. Optional refinement from the same passage: domain = word including suffixes, with enc

sources.quote: 西部裕固语词的重音没有区别词义的作用。重音的位置一般在词的最后音节上。 [...] 不论单音节词或多音节词加附加成分之后，如果增加了音节，重音一般随之往后移。 [...] 但是在语句中，往往由于需要强调某些词，重音就落在该词根或词干的最末音节上，而不在它后面的附加成分上。 (Stress in Western Yugur words has no meaning-distinguishing function. The position of stress is generally on the last syllable of the word. [...] Whether a monosyllabic or a polysyllabic word, after suffixes are added, if the syllable count increases the stress generally moves rightward with them. [...] But in sentences, often because certain words need emphasis, the stress falls on the last syllable of the root or stem and not on the suffix following it.)
sources.locator: examples pu'dzaq 刀子, mo'gəs 角, dava'səq 膀胱, teyer'men; suffixed pu'dzaq -> pudzaq'da, kə'si -> kəsi'ler -> kəsiler'ye; emphatic u'zunluqGca 经常, u'gusden 江的, bu…
sources.note: Word stress on the final syllable, moving rightward onto each added suffix: matches the catalog fixed: final syllable rule (final stress). Stress is stated to be non-contrastive. One stated exception: under sentence-level emphasis stress stays on the stem-final syllable rather than the suffix (u'zunluqGca, u'gusden, bu'yəngə). A further note at printed p. 36 (p. 41): a second-syllable e drops when stress shifts rightward after suffixation. No secondary stress, no weight (vowel length) conditioning, and no lexical tone stated anywhere; the phonology chapter has sections on vowels, consonants,…
